item.title: AI Agent with Almost No AI: The Neural Network Didn't Calculate a Single Ruble in My Estimator
item.description:
In the product called 'AI Estimator,' the neural network hasn't calculated a single ruble yet. A renovation company in Moscow provided five work estimates. The system generated 310 remarks based on them (runs from 16–21.08.2026). The most expensive finding was a total estimate understatement of 515,786 ₽. This understatement was found during the pre-TЗ estimate review, and I wrote the rule for it afterward, so the credit goes to careful reading, not the code. The code is more interesting for other reasons: it produced 51 confirmed remarks beyond the reference list of errors compiled during that review. These were not in the original list. All 310 remarks are generated by the code with rules. The AI layer is written and covered by tests on a stub, but it hasn't run on a live model yet: there's no access key, and the customer chooses the platform. I've provided him with the working version, which operates offline. The second system, a measurement configurator for a service that prepares custom glass shower cabin drawings, has no neural network at all. The model worked in my development environment for both projects: writing code, parsing customer Excel files, and cross-referencing remarks with estimate lines. I only use it in the product where it's indispensable. Read more

item.title: Optimizing a website for neural networks
item.description:
"I asked ChatGPT about your company - it named three competitors." If you work with websites, you've heard this phrase more than once. Even if your site is at the top, traffic from search is good, and conversions are fine. A neural network either doesn't know about you or provides outdated information. The first reaction is to rewrite texts, add expertise, and create an FAQ. We've been through this: the hypothesis of "not enough content" seems logical but is rarely confirmed. The neural network doesn't answer based on your text, but on what reached it. And this is where things get interesting. When we ran our site through queries to various models and examined what their infrastructure actually receives, the picture was prosaic. Some AI crawlers do not execute JavaScript. For a website built in the browser, this means one thing: an empty framework reaches the model instead of an article. The user sees a beautiful page, but the neural network sees an empty file. In this article, we will explore how AI systems read websites, where content gets lost on the way from the server to the model's response, and what can be checked and fixed.

item.title: How Much Does One Hallucination Cost: Calculating the Real Losses from Agent Errors in Production
item.description:
An agent hallucination in production is defined as an incorrect action: an API call, a database write, an email to a client, or a transaction. The cost of such an error is determined not so much by the price of tokens, but by the reversibility of the action and the time it took to notice it. Below are documented cases with sums ranging from $812 to approximately $100 billion in market capitalization, research data, and a formula to estimate the losses from agent errors for your system. item.title: When a Picture is Better Than the Product, or Why Beautiful Visuals Are No Longer Enough in E-commerce
item.description:
When shopping online, a user buys not just the product itself, but also an idea of what it will be like in real life. This idea is increasingly shaped by visuals created or enhanced with AI. Today, sellers can change backgrounds, generate lifestyle scenes, create multiple versions of a main image, or "complete" the surroundings without a full photoshoot in minutes. For businesses, this means faster, cheaper, and more manageable visual content. For users, it means a growing feeling that pictures are becoming harder to trust. If a photo can be significantly improved without changing the product itself, the visual ceases to be a reliable guide for the buyer. Read more

item.title: [Translation] The State of the IT Industry in 2026: What Has Changed, What Broke, and What's Next
item.description:
Gergely Orosz (The Pragmatic Engineer) recaps his talk at the LDX3 conference in New York: what has changed in the industry over the past year, what broke, what remained the same, and where everything is heading. In August 2026, agents created more PRs than humans on GitHub, agents create more tasks than humans in Linear, Cursor and Antigravity moved away from IDEs, and code reviews in many companies have turned into a theater. The article includes fresh data from GitHub, Linear, and Factory AI, stories from OpenAI, Anthropic, Uber, and Ramp. Read more →

item.title: HTTP Request Finished, But LLM Is Still Working: How to Design AI Tasks in Go
item.description:
A typical Go backend is accustomed to canceling work along with the HTTP request. But if a user closes a tab mid-document analysis, it doesn't mean the LLM provider has stopped generation and incurring costs. I'll explain why r.Context() isn't enough for long-running AI operations, how to organize background tasks on PostgreSQL, and what to do about idempotency, retries, and repeated API charges. item.title: Smart Engines and INTELLECT Study: Document Forgery Crimes in Russia Increased by 338%
item.description:
Hello, Habr! We, Smart Engines and the law firm INTELLECT, have completed our annual report on document fraud. The results show a serious deterioration of the situation. In 2025, the number of crimes related to forged documents registered by the Ministry of Internal Affairs increased by 338% year-on-year, reaching a seven-year high. The estimated size of the illegal market for forged identity documents reached 2.6 billion rubles. We discuss the scale of document fraud, new schemes involving generative AI, and technologies for detecting forgeries.
